items.title: Elephants need hairs to STAY COOL
items.claim: Big animals are well-insulated by sheer size — surface area to volume ratio drops as you scale up. So why do elephants have sparse but persistent hairs, in a hot environment where insulation is the last thing they need?
items.prompt: What's the function of an elephant's hairs?

options.text: They INCREASE convective heat loss — the sparse hairs disrupt the still air layer at the skin surface and allow more efficient cooling than bare skin would

items.reveal_title: Surface area scaling and thermal management
items.reveal:
Animal mass scales as length cubed; surface area as length squared. Doubling an animal's linear size doubles its surface-to-volume ratio's inverse — large animals have proportionally less surface area to dump heat through.

Elephants generate huge metabolic heat (about 2500 watts at rest for a 4 tonne adult) but have proportionally tiny skin. They are constantly battling overheating. Their hairs, ears (huge for their body), wallowing in mud, and behavioural cooling all serve heat dissipation.

Cordeschi and colleagues (2012) modelled elephant hair density and showed sparse hairs improve heat loss by about 5 to 20 percent — likely a real evolutionary purpose.
items.why: Hair is associated with warmth. For animals at the wrong end of the surface-to-volume scaling, hair can do the opposite.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: Your entire skeleton is rebuilt every 10 years
items.claim: Bone seems inert. It isn't. Osteoclasts dissolve bone; osteoblasts lay down new bone. The balance maintains structure but constantly turns over the material. In adults, about 10% of bone is replaced each year.
items.prompt: Why turn over a structural tissue at all?

options.text: Continuous remodelling repairs microdamage (fatigue cracks from daily loading), regulates calcium and phosphate balance, and lets bone adapt to changing mechanical demands (Wolff's law)

items.reveal_title: Wolff's law and the calcium reservoir
items.reveal:
Three cell types in bone:
- Osteoblasts: deposit new bone matrix (collagen + hydroxyapatite mineral).
- Osteocytes: mature former osteoblasts embedded in bone matrix; sense mechanical loads.
- Osteoclasts: multinucleate cells that dissolve bone (acid + proteases).

Normal turnover: ~10% of skeleton per year in adults. Trabecular (cancellous) bone turns over faster than cortical bone. Whole-skeleton replacement takes 7-10 years.

Wolff's law (Julius Wolff, 1892): bone adapts to load. Loaded bone strengthens; unloaded bone weakens. Astronauts lose ~1-2% of bone mass per month in microgravity. Bedridden patients similarly. Athletes have denser bones in heavily-used regions (dominant arm of tennis players).

Calcium balance: 99% of body calcium is in bones. The blood calcium pool is small (~10 mmol total) but vital (cardiac function, nerve signalling). Parathyroid hormone mobilises calcium from bone when blood calcium drops; calcitonin reduces calcium release when it rises. Bone is a buffer.

Osteoporosis: net imbalance favouring resorption, especially post-menopause (oestrogen normally restrains osteoclasts). Hip and vertebral fractures rise dramatically.
items.why: Bone looks like stone. Functionally it's a dynamic tissue with continuous renewal, mechanical adaptation, and calcium economy — none of which is visible from the outside but all of which keeps the skeleton viable.
